q: In a call to `pivot_longer()`, what happens to the **names** of the columns selected by `cols`?
choices: They become values in a new column, named by `values_to`
They become the row names of the reshaped result
They are dropped, and only the cell values are kept
They become values in a new column, named by `names_to`
explain: `pivot_longer()` turns column names into data: each selected name is written into the new `names_to` column, and the cells under it go into the `values_to` column. Turning values into column names is the opposite move, `pivot_wider()`.

q: In `pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = prop_ace)`, what role does the `sex` column play?
choices: Its values are what fill the cells of the new columns
It identifies the rows, so each sex gets its own row
Its distinct values become the names of the new columns
It names a new column that holds the old column names
explain: `names_from` supplies the new column names (one column per sex) and `values_from` supplies the cell contents. Rows are identified by `id_cols`, which by default are all the columns not named in `names_from` or `values_from`.

q:
The Billboard data has one row per song, with weekly chart positions in columns `wk1` to `wk76`. Fill in the blank so the chart positions end up in a column called `rank`:
```r
billboard |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    ____ = "rank"
  )
```
explain: `values_to` names the new column that receives the cell values, just as `names_to` names the one that receives the old column names. `values_from` and `names_from` are `pivot_wider()` arguments, and `names_prefix` strips text from the old names.

q:
What does `names_prefix = "wk"` do in this call?
```r
billboard |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",
    values_to = "rank"
  )
```
choices: Strips the leading `wk` from each name, so `week` holds `"1"`, `"2"`, …
Selects the columns that start with `wk`, so `cols` is no longer needed
Converts `week` to an integer column holding the numbers 1 through 76
Drops the rows where a song has no rank in that week
explain: `names_prefix` removes matching text from the start of each column name before it is stored in `week`. The values are still character strings; turning them into numbers is the job of `names_transform`, and dropping missing ranks is `values_drop_na`.

q:
Both extra arguments are used here:
```r
billboard |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",
    names_transform = as.integer,
    values_to = "rank"
  )
```
Compared with deleting only the `names_transform` line, what is different about the result?
choices: `rank` is an integer column instead of a double column
The `wk` prefix is removed, which `names_prefix` alone does not do
The rows are sorted by week number instead of by song
`week` is an integer column instead of a character column
explain: `names_transform` is applied to the new `names_to` column after the prefix is stripped, turning `"1"`, `"2"`, … into the integers 1, 2, …. It never touches the cell values (that would be `values_transform`) and does not reorder rows.

q:
A student keeps `names_transform = as.integer` but forgets `names_prefix`:
```r
billboard |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_transform = as.integer,
    values_to = "rank"
  )
```
What ends up in `week`?
choices: The integers 1 to 76, since `as.integer()` skips the letters
The strings `"wk1"` to `"wk76"`, since the transform is ignored
`NA` in every row, along with a warning about coercion
Nothing: the call errors because `names_prefix` is required
explain: The transform is applied to the full names, and `as.integer("wk1")` is `NA` (R warns that NAs were introduced by coercion). Strip the prefix first with `names_prefix = "wk"` so the names are `"1"`, `"2"`, … before converting.

q: With `names_prefix = "wk"` but no `names_transform`, the Billboard `week` column holds the strings `"1"`, `"2"`, …, `"76"`. Why is it worth converting it to integer?
choices: `pivot_wider()` cannot use a character column as its `names_from`
As text it sorts `"10"` before `"2"`, and it is treated as categories, not numbers
`pivot_longer()` will not finish until `week` has a numeric type
The `rank` values stay stored as text until `week` is converted
explain: Character values compare letter by letter, so `"10"` comes before `"2"`, and a character `week` gives a discrete plot axis in that alphabetical order (1, 10, 11, …, 2, 20, …). `names_transform = as.integer` makes week a real number.

q:
`songs`:
```
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  track        wk1   wk2   wk3
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Breathe       81    68    50
2 Kryptonite    74    61    NA
```
What is the **fourth** row of the result?
```r
songs |>
  pivot_longer(cols = wk1:wk3, names_to = "week", values_to = "rank")
```
explain: `pivot_longer()` walks through the original rows in order and, within each row, through the pivoted columns: Breathe `wk1`, `wk2`, `wk3`, then Kryptonite `wk1`, `wk2`, `wk3`. Stacking column by column would put Kryptonite `wk2` fourth, but that is not tidyr's order.

q:
`quiz` has 3 rows and 6 columns: `student`, `section`, and the scores `q1`, `q2`, `q3`, `q4`. What are the dimensions of the result?
```r
quiz |>
  pivot_longer(cols = q1:q4, names_to = "question", values_to = "points")
```
explain: Each of the 3 rows becomes 4 rows, one per pivoted column: \( 3 \times 4 = 12 \). The untouched `student` and `section` are kept, and `question` and `points` are added, so there are 4 columns.

q:
`billboard` is a 317 × 79 tibble: `artist`, `track`, `date.entered`, and `wk1` through `wk76`. What are the dimensions of the result?
```r
billboard |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("wk"), names_to = "week", values_to = "rank")
```
explain: One row per song per pivoted column: \( 317 \times 76 = 24{,}092 \). The 3 identifier columns stay and `week` and `rank` are added, giving 5 columns. Multiplying by all 79 columns is the classic slip.

q: Adding `values_drop_na = TRUE` to the Billboard `pivot_longer()` call cuts the result from 24,092 rows to 5,307. What do the removed rows represent?
choices: Songs that charted for fewer than 76 weeks, removed entirely
Song-weeks in which the song was not on the chart
Duplicate song-weeks that the pivot created by mistake
Weeks after each song had already left the top 10
explain: In the wide table a song that charted for 20 weeks has `NA` in its other 56 `wk` columns. Pivoting turns each of those cells into a row with a missing rank, and `values_drop_na = TRUE` removes just those rows; every song keeps the weeks it was on the chart.

q: You want a line plot of each Billboard song's rank (y) against week (x), one line per song. Why does the data have to be pivoted longer first?
choices: `aes(x = week)` needs week in one column, but it is spread across 76 column names
`ggplot()` refuses tibbles with more than a few dozen columns
`geom_line()` needs rows pre-sorted by rank, which only the long form has
`ggplot()` cannot draw anything from a table that contains `NA`
explain: ggplot2 maps aesthetics to variables stored in columns. In the wide table, week isn't a column at all; it lives in 76 column names, so there is nothing to map to x. After pivoting, `aes(x = week, y = rank, group = track)` works directly.

q:
Which call turns `gdp_wide` into `gdp_long`?
`gdp_wide`:
```
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  country `2019` `2020`
  <chr>    <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Chile      279    254
2 Peru       228    202
```
`gdp_long`:
```
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  country year    gdp
  <chr>   <chr> <dbl>
1 Chile   2019    279
2 Chile   2020    254
3 Peru    2019    228
4 Peru    2020    202
```
explain: The old column names `2019` and `2020` land in `year` (`names_to = "year"`) and the cells land in `gdp` (`values_to = "gdp"`); `cols = -country` stacks everything except the identifier. `year` comes out as character because it was made from column names.

q:
`gdp_wide` has the columns `country`, `2019`, `2020`, `2021`. Fill in the blank to stack the three year columns:
```r
gdp_wide |>
  pivot_longer(____, names_to = "year", values_to = "gdp")
```
explain: `cols` selects the columns to stack, and `-country` means every column except `country`. `cols = country` would stack the identifier instead, `"year"` is not a column yet (it names the new one), and `names_from` is a `pivot_wider()` argument.

q:
`gdp_wide` has a character column `country` and numeric columns `2019` and `2020`. Why does this call stop with an error?
```r
gdp_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "year", values_to = "gdp")
```
choices: `everything()` cannot be used to choose columns inside `pivot_longer()`
It tries to put `country` text and numeric GDP values into the same `gdp` column
`names_to` must name an existing column, and there is no `year` column
Columns whose names are numbers, like `2019`, cannot be pivoted at all
explain: `everything()` includes `country`, so its character values would have to share one value column with doubles, and `pivot_longer()` refuses to combine the two types. Leave the identifier out with `cols = -country`.

q:
`long` was made with
```r
long <- wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -country, names_to = "year", values_to = "cases")
```
Which call puts `long` back in the original layout?
explain: `pivot_wider()` is the inverse of `pivot_longer()`: the column that `names_to` created supplies the new column names (`names_from = year`) and the one `values_to` created supplies the cells (`values_from = cases`). The others swap those roles or borrow `pivot_longer()` argument names.

q: `long` was made with `pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("wk"), names_to = "week", names_prefix = "wk", values_to = "rank")`. Pivoting it back with `pivot_wider(long, names_from = week, values_from = rank)` gives columns named `1`, `2`, `3`, …. Which extra argument to `pivot_wider()` brings back the names `wk1`, `wk2`, …?
explain: In `pivot_wider()`, `names_prefix` is a string pasted onto the front of every new column name, the mirror image of `pivot_longer()`, where it is stripped off. `names_sep` only joins the pieces when several columns build each name.

q:

```
   <fct>     <chr>     <dbl>
```

Fill in the blanks to get one row per health category and one column per sex:
```r
ace_summary |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = ____, values_from = ____)
```
explain: The values of `sex` become the column names and `prop_ace` fills the cells; the leftover column, `genhlth`, identifies the rows. `names_from = genhlth` would instead give one row per sex and one column per health category.

q: `ace_summary` has 10 rows and 3 columns: `genhlth` (5 categories), `sex` (Female, Male), and `prop_ace`. What are the dimensions of `pivot_wider(ace_summary, names_from = sex, values_from = prop_ace)`?

q: In HW1, the grouped summary of ACE proportions by general health and sex was pivoted wider before it was displayed. What is that step for?
choices: Females and males sit side by side, so they're easy to compare in each category
The `summarize()` output is untidy, and widening it is what makes it tidy
ggplot2 needs a separate column for each sex to color the bars by sex
The wide table stores fewer numbers, so its proportions are more precise
explain: The long summary is already tidy, and it's the one to plot (with `fill = sex`). The wide version holds the same 10 proportions, laid out for a human reader who scans across a row to compare the sexes.

Starting from the 10-row `ace_summary` (columns `genhlth`, `sex`, `prop_ace`), which call produces this table?

```
  sex    Excellent `Very good`  Good  Fair  Poor

1 Female      0.55        0.61  0.63  0.69  0.74
2 Male        0.49        0.53  0.56  0.61  0.66
```
explain: The health categories became column names, so they came from `names_from = genhlth`, and the cells are proportions (`values_from = prop_ace`). With those two used up, `sex` is the identifier, giving one row per sex.

q:
In the HW2 SEDA data, `gap` holds two kinds of measurement, a math gap and a reading (`rla`) gap, told apart by `subject`:
```
# A tibble: 4 × 4
     id grade subject   gap
  <dbl> <dbl> <chr>   <dbl>
1   101     3 math     0.12
2   101     3 rla     -0.21
3   101     4 math     0.15
4   101     4 rla     -0.18
```
Which call gives one row per district-grade, with separate `math` and `rla` columns?
explain: The subject labels become column names (`names_from = subject`) and the gap estimates fill them (`values_from = gap`); `id` and `grade` stay as identifiers, so both subjects for a district-grade land in one row. There are no `math` or `rla` columns to stack yet.

q: A long SEDA table has one row per district × grade × subject (500 districts, grades 3–8, math and rla) and the columns `id`, `grade`, `subject`, `gap`. What are its dimensions after `pivot_wider(names_from = subject, values_from = gap)`?
explain: The long table has \( 500 \times 6 \times 2 = 6{,}000 \) rows; widening by subject leaves one row per district-grade, \( 500 \times 6 = 3{,}000 \). `subject` and `gap` are replaced by `math` and `rla`, so the columns are `id`, `grade`, `math`, `rla`.

q:
This version of the SEDA data also has a standard error `se` for each gap:
```
# A tibble: 4 × 5
     id grade subject   gap    se
  <dbl> <dbl> <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1   101     3 math     0.12  0.04
2   101     3 rla     -0.21  0.05
3   101     4 math     0.15  0.03
4   101     4 rla     -0.18  0.06
```
What does `pivot_wider(seda, names_from = subject, values_from = gap)` return?
choices: 4 rows: `se` acts as an identifier, so math and rla never share a row
2 rows, one per district-grade, with the `se` column silently dropped
2 rows, one per district-grade, with `se` averaged over the subjects
An error, because `se` is not named in `values_from`
explain: By default `id_cols` is every column not used in `names_from` or `values_from`: here `id`, `grade`, and `se`. Every row has a different `se`, so every row stays separate, giving a staircase with `math` filled and `rla` `NA` in one row, and the reverse in the next.

q: Using the same SEDA table (`id`, `grade`, `subject`, `gap`, `se`), which call returns one row per district-grade with exactly the columns `id`, `grade`, `math`, `rla`?
choices: `pivot_wider(seda, id_cols = c(id, grade, se), names_from = subject, values_from = gap)`
`pivot_wider(seda, id_cols = se, names_from = subject, values_from = gap)`
`pivot_wider(seda, id_cols = c(id, grade), names_from = subject, values_from = gap)`
explain: `id_cols = c(id, grade)` says only those columns identify a row, so `se` is dropped and the two subjects collapse into one row. Keeping `se` among the ids still gives the 4-row staircase, and putting `se` in `names_from` creates columns like `math_0.04`.

q:
Using the same SEDA table (`id`, `grade`, `subject`, `gap`, `se`), what columns does this return?
```r
seda |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = subject, values_from = c(gap, se))
```
explain: With two value columns, each new name is the value column's name, an underscore, and the subject, so both `gap` and `se` get a math and an rla version, and the rows collapse to one per district-grade. It's a common fix when each estimate has its own standard error.

`gdp_long`:

37 under `2020`; the `2019` column is dropped for every country

q:
A student drops `grade` from the SEDA table before widening, leaving `no_grade`:
```
# A tibble: 4 × 3
     id subject   gap
  <dbl> <chr>   <dbl>
1   101 math     0.12
2   101 rla     -0.21
3   101 math     0.15
4   101 rla     -0.18
```
What does `pivot_wider(no_grade, names_from = subject, values_from = gap)` do?
choices: Returns one row, with list-columns `math` and `rla` holding two gaps each, and warns
Returns two rows for district 101, one for each grade, as before
Returns one row, with each subject's two gaps averaged together
Returns one row, keeping only the first gap for each subject
explain: Without `grade`, `id` and `subject` no longer pin down a single `gap`: district 101 has two math values. `pivot_wider()` won't guess, so it stores both in a list-column and warns that the values are not uniquely identified. Keep every identifying column.

q: Each table below holds tuberculosis data by country and year. Which one needs `pivot_longer()` to become tidy?
choices: Columns `country`, `1999`, `2000`, with case counts under each year
explain: Values of a variable (years) sitting in column names is the signal for `pivot_longer()`. The `type`/`count` table has the opposite problem, two variables stacked in one column, fixed by `pivot_wider()`; the `cases`/`population` table is already tidy; `rate` needs splitting, not pivoting.

q: To compute, for each district-grade, the difference between its math gap and its reading gap, why pivot the long SEDA table (one row per district × grade × subject) wider first?
choices: `mutate()` cannot do arithmetic on a column next to a character column
The long table is untidy, and `mutate()` refuses untidy input
`mutate()` works within a row, and the two gaps start out in different rows
Widening sorts the rows so that math and rla rows alternate
explain: `mutate()` computes from values in the same row. After `pivot_wider(names_from = subject, values_from = gap)` each district-grade has `math` and `rla` side by side, so `mutate(diff = math - rla)` works directly.

q: Why is it `names_to = "week"` (quoted) in `pivot_longer()`, but `names_from = week` (bare) in `pivot_wider()`?
choices: Quoting makes the new column character, while a bare name would make it numeric
`names_to` names a column that doesn't exist yet; `names_from` refers to an existing one
`pivot_longer()` uses base R evaluation, while `pivot_wider()` uses tidy evaluation
Bare column names only work once a pipe `|>` has supplied the data frame
explain: Arguments that pick existing columns (`cols`, `names_from`, `values_from`, `id_cols`) use tidy selection, so bare names work. `names_to` and `values_to` name columns that will be created, so they take strings; the column's type comes from the data, not the quotes.

q: When joining `gdp` and `pop` (each with one row per country-year), `country` and `year` together serve as the key. What makes them the key?
choices: They are the columns used to match each row of one table to rows of the other
They are the only columns with no missing values in either table
They come first in both tables, and joins always match on leading columns
They are the columns the join copies over from the second table
explain: A key is whatever column or columns you match rows on; the join pairs rows whose key values are equal. One country-year identifies a row here, so both columns are needed: matching on `country` alone would pair each GDP year with every population year.

q: `inner_join()`, `left_join()`, `right_join()`, and `full_join()` can all be run with the same key. What does choosing among them decide?
choices: Which columns are used to match rows between the two tables
Whether a key that matches several rows gets duplicated
Whether key columns are compared as text or as numbers
What happens to rows whose key has no match in the other table
explain: The key says how rows are matched; the join type is the rule for unmatched rows: drop them (inner), keep the first table's (left), keep the second table's (right), or keep both (full). In every type, a key that matches several rows gives one output row per match.

q: You want GDP per person for exactly the country-years that have both a GDP value and a population value, with no rows padded by `NA`. Which call gives that table?
explain: An inner join keeps only keys found in both tables, so every row has both numbers and `gdp / pop` is never `NA`. Left, right, and full joins keep some unmatched keys and fill the missing side with `NA`.

q: `right_join(gdp, pop, by = c("country", "year"))` keeps the same rows as which other call?
explain: Both keep every row of `pop` and put `NA` in `gdp` where there's no match; only the column order (and possibly the row order) differs. `left_join(gdp, pop)` keeps every row of `gdp` instead.

q: Tables `x` and `y` share a column `key`. In `x` it holds A, B, C; in `y` it holds B, C, D; no value repeats. Which call returns rows for exactly B, C, and D?
explain: A right join keeps every key of the second table (B, C, D), with `NA` in `x`'s columns for D. `left_join()` gives A, B, C; `inner_join()` gives B, C; `full_join()` gives A through D.

q: True or false: swapping the two tables in an inner join (`inner_join(y, x)` instead of `inner_join(x, y)`) changes which keys appear in the result.
explain: An inner join keeps the keys found in both tables, and being in both doesn't depend on the order. Swapping only changes the column (and row) order. For `left_join()` the order matters, since it decides which table keeps all its rows.

q: True or false: `left_join(x, y)` always returns exactly `nrow(x)` rows.
explain: It returns at least `nrow(x)` rows. Any row of `x` whose key matches several rows of `y` is repeated once per match, so the row count grows unless the key is unique in `y`.

q: `gdp2020` has one row per country for 190 countries, and `pop2020` has one row per country for 200 countries; 185 countries appear in both. How many rows does `full_join(gdp2020, pop2020, by = "country")` return?
explain: The 185 shared countries, plus 5 found only in `gdp2020` and 15 only in `pop2020`: \( 185 + 5 + 15 = 205 \). An inner join would give 185, a left join 190, and a right join 200.

q:
In HW2, district-by-grade gaps were joined to district-by-grade covariates (`ses` is socioeconomic status).
`gaps`:

```
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1   101     3  0.12 -0.21
2   101     4  0.15 -0.18
3   102     3  0.05 -0.31
4   102     4  0.08 -0.25
```

`covars`:
```
# A tibble: 4 × 3
     id grade   ses
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1   101     3  0.42
2   101     4  0.47
3   102     3 -1.13
4   102     4 -0.95
```
Fill in the blank so rows are matched on both district and grade:
```r
left_join(gaps, covars, by = ____)
```
explain: `by` takes a character vector of key names, so `c("id", "grade")` matches on district and grade together (`join_by(id, grade)` is equivalent). `c("id" = "grade")` would match `gaps$id` to `covars$grade`, and bare `c(id, grade)` looks for R objects named `id` and `grade`.

q: Suppose `covars` calls the district ID `district` instead of `id`, so its columns are `district`, `grade`, `ses`. Which call matches `gaps` (columns `id`, `grade`, `math`, `rla`) to `covars` on district and grade?
explain: In `join_by()`, `id == district` pairs a column of the left table with a differently named column of the right, and plain `grade` means the same name on both sides; `by = c("id" = "district", "grade")` is the older equivalent. Listing `id` and `district` as separate keys fails, since each table lacks one of them.

q: `gaps` has columns `id`, `grade`, `math`, `rla`, and `covars` has `district`, `grade`, `ses`. What columns does `left_join(gaps, covars, join_by(id == district, grade))` return?
explain: Matched key columns hold the same values, so dplyr keeps one copy under the left table's name (`id`) and then adds the right table's non-key columns. The `.x`/`.y` suffixes appear only for non-key columns that share a name.

q: The SEDA `gaps` and `covars` tables each have 3,000 rows: 500 districts × 6 grades, one row per district-grade. How many rows does `left_join(gaps, covars, by = "id")` return?

q: Some district-grades in `gaps` have no row in `covars`. You want every row of `gaps` kept, with `ses` set to `NA` where covariates are missing. Which call?
explain: A left join keeps every row of its first table and fills the second table's columns with `NA` where there is no match. The inner join drops the unmatched district-grades, and the last two keep all of `covars` instead.

`gdp`:

```
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 Chile    2019   279
```

`pop2` accidentally lists Chile 2020 twice, from two sources:
```
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  country  year   pop
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 Chile    2019  18.9
2 Chile    2020  19.3
3 Chile    2020  19.5
```

What does `left_join(gdp, pop2, by = c("country", "year"))` return?
choices: 4 rows, keeping the first Chile 2020 population
4 rows, with the two Chile 2020 populations averaged
5 rows, with Chile's 2020 GDP of 254 appearing twice
An error, because a key appears twice in `pop2`
explain: A left join keeps every `gdp` row, and a row whose key matches two `pop2` rows comes out twice, once per match (Peru 2019 still gets `NA`). A total of GDP computed afterwards would count Chile 2020 twice, so check that keys are unique in the lookup table first.

q: Before running `left_join(gaps, covars, by = c("id", "grade"))`, you want to be sure the result will have exactly `nrow(gaps)` rows. Which check guarantees that?
choices: `gaps |> count(id, grade) |> filter(n > 1)` returns no rows
`covars |> count(id, grade) |> filter(n > 1)` returns no rows
explain: A left join adds rows only when a key matches several rows of the right table, so the key must be unique in `covars`. Repeated keys in `gaps` are just carried through, equal row counts don't rule out duplicates, and `%in%` checks for matches, not uniqueness.

q: What does `left_join(gdp, pop)` do when `by` is left out?
choices: Joins on every column name the two tables share, here `country` and `year`
Joins on just the first column of each table, which here is `country`
Matches rows by position: row 1 with row 1, row 2 with row 2, and so on
Stops with an error, because `by` is a required argument of every join
explain: With no `by`, dplyr does a natural join on all columns with the same name and prints a message naming them (`join_by(country, year)`). That's right here, but a shared column that isn't meant as a key gets matched too, so it's safer to spell out `by`.

q: Both `gdp` and `pop` have a `source` column (`"WB"` in every `gdp` row, `"UN"` in every `pop` row). `left_join(gdp, pop)` runs without error, but `pop` is `NA` in every row. Why?
choices: A left join fills `pop` only when both tables have the same number of rows
The `source` columns were renamed `source.x` and `source.y`, breaking the match
Without `by`, `left_join()` adds the columns of `pop` but never fills them
With no `by`, `source` was used as a key too, and no source value matches
explain: A natural join matches on all shared columns, so rows had to agree on `country`, `year`, and `source`; `"WB"` never equals `"UN"`, so nothing matched. Use `by = c("country", "year")`; the two `source` columns then come through as `source.x` and `source.y`.

q:
`gdp` uses country names (`Chile`, `Peru`), but a new population table uses country codes:
```
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  country  year   pop
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 CHL      2019  18.9
2 CHL      2020  19.3
3 PER      2020  33.3
4 BOL      2020  11.9
```
`inner_join(gdp, pop_codes, by = c("country", "year"))` returns 0 rows. Why?
choices: `inner_join()` needs both tables sorted by country and year first
Keys must be character columns, and `year` is numeric
Keys must match exactly, and `"Chile"` is not equal to `"CHL"`
An inner join drops every country that is missing a year in either table
explain: Joins compare key values for exact equality, so names never match codes and an inner join keeps nothing (a left join would keep every `gdp` row with `pop` all `NA`). Recode one table, for example with a names-to-codes lookup, before joining.

q: In `covars`, `grade` was read in as character (`"3"`, `"4"`, …), while in `gaps` it is numeric. What happens with `left_join(gaps, covars, by = c("id", "grade"))`?
choices: It converts both `grade` columns to text and joins normally
An error saying `grade` has incompatible types in the two tables
It runs, but `ses` is `NA` in every row because no grade matches
It quietly joins on `id` alone and ignores the `grade` key
explain: dplyr won't compare numbers with strings in a key; it stops and reports that `x$grade` is a double and `y$grade` is a character. Convert one side first, for example `mutate(grade = as.numeric(grade))` on `covars`.

q:
`seda_long` has 3,000 rows (250 districts × grades 3–8 × math and rla) with columns `id`, `grade`, `subject`, `gap`. `covars` has one row for each of the 1,500 district-grades, with columns `id`, `grade`, `ses`. What are the dimensions of the result?
```r
seda_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = subject, values_from = gap) |>
  left_join(covars, by = c("id", "grade"))
```
explain: Widening by subject leaves one row per district-grade: 1,500 rows with `id`, `grade`, `math`, `rla`. Each of those matches exactly one `covars` row on the two keys, so the join keeps 1,500 rows and adds `ses`, for 5 columns.
